name: Umar Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by telling me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior line cook at the Harbour View Hotel restaurant, on the seafront. In summer it's two hundred covers a night, covers meaning plates of food, and I'm on the sauté pans next to Lucia, who runs the section. I burn the odd shallot still, she shouts, I learn. I love the speed of it when the tickets are flying.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Winter. From November the hotel goes half empty and they drop me to twenty hours. I share a flat above a phone shop with my mate Tomas, and my half of the rent is more than half my winter pay. There's only two other kitchens in town that hire all year, and they're full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, I never thought a computer was going to sauté mushrooms anyway. With the lads in the kitchen I'd joke that the hotel's booking website is still broken, so much for AI. Online I'd say the real story is seasonal work and nobody fixing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing gets better for me. I still lose half my hours every November and I still have less than a month's rent put away. The thing that's going to hurt me this winter is the same thing that hurt me last winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, do the summer season properly and ask Lucia to teach me the fish station so I'm more useful. I'd look for winter shifts at the care home kitchen up the hill, which pays badly but it's something. And I'd stop sending money to my brother for a few months, which I hate doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, like nothing's coming to save me, but nothing's coming to wreck me either. Mostly tired of being broke every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did last winter actually look like, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had about three hundred left on the first of December and rent was due on the fifth. I borrowed from Tomas and paid him back in April. I ate a lot of hotel staff meals I wasn't strictly supposed to take home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to turn my gran's fish stew recipe from Portuguese into English, and to tidy my CV. I wouldn't trust it to plan a menu, though, it doesn't taste anything.

say: I'd joke that the hotel's **booking website** is still broken, so much for AI.
I'd say online that the real story is **seasonal work** nobody fixes.
think: I still lose **half my hours** every November, AI or not.
I have **less than a month's** rent saved, and that doesn't change.
do: Ask the section lead to teach me the **fish station** this summer.
Look for **winter shifts** at the care home kitchen up the hill.
Pause the money I send **my brother** for a few months.
feel: **Flat**, with nothing coming to save me or wreck me.
S0.quote: The thing that's going to hurt me this winter is the same thing that hurt me last winter.
fieldNote: Umar's real threat is the **seasonal hour cut**, which AI Plateau leaves untouched.
He borrowed from his flatmate last winter, so his **cushion is negative** in practice.
He uses AI **casually and practically**, for a recipe and a CV.

steps.text: Learn the fish station from the section lead this summer
Apply for winter shifts at the care home kitchen up the hill
Pause money sent to his brother for three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the hotel office that changes, not the pass. Booking, rotas, the supplier orders, I'd say that's where the jobs go. Online I'd say the savings should go to the staff, not the shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it squeezes me sideways. If the hotel saves money on reception and admin, maybe they keep the restaurant open more in winter, or maybe they just pocket it. And if they use software to plan the rota to the minute, my twenty winter hours could become fifteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other cooks do first, then copy what works. If the head chef starts using an ordering app, I'd ask to learn it so I'm not the one left behind. I'd also join the hospitality union, because rota software is exactly the kind of thing a union should have a say on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the stomach. Not scared, more like watching the tide come in a bit higher each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rota software cutting hours. Has anything like that happened yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At my last job, a chain burger place, an app sent people home early if sales dropped. You'd get a message at seven saying you're done. That's why I left, and why I'd fight it here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the hotel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia on reception, she's been there twelve years and does all the bookings by phone. If the website and a chatbot take that, she's out. She brings us leftover cake from the conference room.

say: I'd say the **hotel office** changes first, not the pass.
I'd argue savings should go to **staff, not shareholders**.
think: Rota software could turn **twenty winter hours** into fifteen.
Hotel savings might keep the **restaurant open** in winter, or just disappear into profit.
do: Watch the other cooks, then **copy what works** with new tools.
Ask the head chef to teach me the **ordering app** once it arrives.
Join the **hospitality union** to get a say on rota software.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the tide coming in higher each year.
S1.quote: At my last job, a chain burger place, an app sent people home early if sales dropped. You'd get a message at seven saying you're done.
fieldNote: Umar's fear is **scheduling software** cutting his already thin winter hours.
He waits for proof, then **follows others**, which fits his steady habit.
A past job with **app-driven send-homes** shapes his support for the union.

steps.text: Ask the head chef to teach him the new ordering app
Join the hospitality union and raise rota software at a meeting
Watch how other cooks use new tools before copying them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we needed rules years ago. At work I'd say we stick together. Online I'd be angry, I'd share everything about a basic income, money paid to everyone, because what else is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years and the booking, ordering and menus are done by AI, and three years after that a robot can do my pans. I'm twenty-seven, I didn't finish school, and the only thing I'm half good at is cooking. By thirty-two I could be out with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting for once. In the first months I'd look into a course in fixing kitchen equipment, combi ovens and fryers, because someone has to fix the robots. I'd move back in with my mum if the hotel cut winter hours again, and I'd save every summer pay packet I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor tilting. I'm usually a wait-and-see person, but this doesn't give me time to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move back with your mum. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. She's got a two-bed flat with my little brother in the other room, so I'd be on the sofa. She'd be glad, and I'd feel like I'd gone backwards five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why repair work rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Frank, the engineer who fixes the hotel dishwasher, says he's booked for weeks. Machines break in kitchens all the time, steam and grease kill them. If there's going to be robots in every kitchen, someone's got to keep the robots alive.

say: I'd say this is why we needed **rules years ago**.
I'd share everything about a **basic income** for everyone.
think: Robots could do **my pans** by about 2031, when I'm thirty-two.
I left school early and **cooking is all** I'm half good at.
do: Look into a **kitchen equipment repair** course in the first months.
Move back in with **my mum** if winter hours drop again.
Save **every summer pay packet** I can.
feel: Like the **floor tilting**, with no time to wait and see.
S2.quote: If there's going to be robots in every kitchen, someone's got to keep the robots alive.
fieldNote: The fast timeline forces Umar out of his **wait-and-see** habit.
He reasons from a **real person**, the hotel's repair engineer, towards a new trade.
Moving back to his mum's sofa feels like **going backwards**, which stings.

steps.text: Enrol on a kitchen equipment repair course at the college
Move back to his mum's two-bed flat if winter hours drop
Bank most of each summer pay packet from the hotel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if the government actually helps. In the kitchen I'd say start learning something now, don't wait. Online I'd push for free retraining for people who left school early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years plus three for robots means I've got about eight years cooking. That's long enough to get good at the fish station and then get out. I'm not panicking, but I know it's coming for my pans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give it a year of watching how fast it moves, then sign up for the equipment repair course in the evenings. I'd ask Frank if I can shadow him on a couple of call-outs. And I'd try hard to get a few months' rent saved, which I've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but with a plan. Better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch for a year first. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the big chains start putting in robot fryers and wok machines. If the burger place on the bypass gets a robot fryer, that's my sign to sign up for the course. I'd rather see it work before I pay for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your winters in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same, twenty hours and borrowing. Unless the shadowing with Frank turns into paid work in the quiet months. That would be the dream, honestly.

say: I'd say **five years is enough** if the government actually helps.
I'd push for **free retraining** for people who left school early.
think: I've got about **eight years cooking** before robots reach my pans.
Enough time to master the **fish station** and then get out.
do: Watch the big chains for **robot fryers** for a year before acting.
Start the **repair course** in the evenings after that.
Shadow the hotel's **repair engineer** on a couple of call-outs.
S3.quote: If the burger place on the bypass gets a robot fryer, that's my sign to sign up for the course.
fieldNote: Umar sets himself a **clear trigger**, a robot fryer at a nearby chain.
The extra years let him fall back to his **steady, watch-first** style.
He hopes the repair shadowing becomes **winter income**.

steps.text: Watch whether the bypass burger place installs a robot fryer
Take an evening kitchen equipment repair course
Shadow the hotel's repair engineer for paid winter call-outs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disaster if we don't. In the staff room I'd tell the younger ones not to plan a whole life on the pans. Online I'd say this is when the government should build colleges, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three is thirteen, so I'm forty when the robot cooks arrive. That's a long time to keep doing something I like. But I know by forty I'd want a trade that isn't seasonal, so the robots just push me towards a decision I'd need anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first couple of years getting properly good, maybe a cooking certificate at college. Then I'd do the repair course around year three, once I've seen who's buying what machines. I'd keep the hotel job until the repair work pays enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, though I know I'll still be broke every winter for a while. It's like having a long run-up to a jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots push you to a decision you'd need anyway. What's that decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting off seasonal work. Every winter I borrow, every summer I pay back, and I'm twenty-seven doing that. Ten years of warning makes me finally sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the younger cooks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the sixteen-year-old pot washers to learn the machines as well as the knives. The kitchen in 2039 won't look like this one. They'll laugh at me, but I'd say it.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift or a disaster**, depending on what we do.
I'd say now is when governments should **build colleges**, not later.
think: I'm **forty** when robot cooks arrive, which is a long run in a job I like.
The robots push me off **seasonal work**, a choice I'd need anyway.
do: Get a **cooking certificate** at college in the first two years.
Start the **repair course** around year three, once the machines are clear.
Keep the **hotel job** until repair work pays enough.
feel: **Calmer**, like a long run-up to a jump.
Still **braced for broke winters** for a while.
S4.quote: I'd tell the sixteen-year-old pot washers to learn the machines as well as the knives.
fieldNote: Umar treats the long timeline as a reason to **finally leave seasonal work**.
He still expects **broke winters**, so the mood stays anxious despite the plan.
He plans in **stages**, which matches his steady approach.

steps.text: Earn a vocational cooking certificate at college within two years
Keep working summers at the Harbour View Hotel while studying

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to learn a new trade and no money to live on while I did. What would help is a free course I can do in the winter when the hotel's dead, with some money to live on while I do it. And proper winter hours, but I know that's a separate fight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. My brother's sixteen and wants to be a chef because of me. I don't know what to tell my brother now.

headlineQuote: My brother's sixteen and wants to be a chef because of me. I don't know what to tell my brother now.
portrait: Umar is a 27-year-old **junior line cook** at a seaside hotel restaurant, on sauté in summer.
He loses **half his hours** every winter and borrows from his flatmate to cover rent.
He leans progressive, backs **unions and public retraining**, and uses AI now and then.
He waits for proof, but fast AGI forces him towards **kitchen equipment repair**.
His moods sit at anxious to alarmed because **seasonal pay** never feels safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time or money to learn a new trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **free winter course** with living money while he studies.
**Year-round hours** at the hotel, which he calls a separate fight.
